title: Adrift
summary: A lone survivor lives his final moments aboard a ship drifting through the cosmos
html:
The red emergency lights flickered along the hall as Anastas pulled himself along the wall and entered the observatory. He peered out of the thick glass window into a field of stars. Parts of the window were obscured by the red streaks that stained the glass and the frame around it. Hundreds of thousands of stars peaked through the window and lit the observatory dimly, the light tinted ever so slightly red by the nearest star, an ancient ball of gas resting far beyond his reach. A dim light from behind him drew his attention.

A ghostly form of Captain Ivanov sat in the seat by the conference table. While Anastas approached, the shadow of Major Dmitriyev came up and stood behind Captain Ivanov.

“I don’t like this project, Gavriil. But the League will not listen to us. America is determined to obtain Powder by any means necessary, and we are only a hindrance to them. In time, they might push us aside entirely if we keep interfering.”

Major Dmitriyev paced on the floor behind him. “The future has arrived, Captain. Eternal life, post-scarcity, the utopia of our dreams and the dreams of our ancestors and their ancestors since time immemorial, it might finally be within our reach. And yet…”

Anastas reached out and passed his hand through the ghost of the captain.

“And yet, Gavriil?”

“And yet I fear you are right, Fyodor. I have spoken to the Americans. Most are eager to begin humanity’s new, great adventure into the stars. Most. I spoke to general Watchman. His father told him of realms we cannot possibly understand. We do not know what we are unleashing on our world.”

And they were gone. The table was silent and empty, and Anastas was left alone in the room.

Anastas drifted back into the hallway and navigated to communications. The intercom was useless, of course, and the power was nearly gone anyways. Anastas powered on the broadcaster to send one more message.

“I am Anastas Petrovich of Asia Station, third station of Project Eternity, and final known survivor of the same. It has been seven days or so since the incursion on our world. The station as far as I know was destroyed; save this section alone. I was cast through a rift into deep space; I don’t know where I am, or who can hear me. But if any sentient life can hear my message, if you can understand my words, I am no threat to you. Our home was ripped apart by forces beyond our comprehension, and I may be the last of my species. If humanity still exists in this cosmos, I am here and alive, but perhaps not for much longer — for I am running out of air.”

He repeated himself in English, German, and Spanish, then shut down the broadcaster.

The emergency lights blinked feebly as he maneuvered through the dim hallway and past the observatory. An unearthly glow flowed about the room as he glanced through the door while passing. At the end of the hall, Anastas strapped himself to the wall and drifted off to sleep.

It could have been three hours later or thirteen when Anastas awoke from dreaming of fire and portals. He tried to check his watch, but it was too dark. Anastas slowly came to his senses and realized the emergency lights had gone out. The open door to the observatory spilled a taste of star light across the threshold in a feeble attempt to push back total darkness. A brighter light moved slowly past the doorway, and he noticed voices in the observatory.

“Has it been twelve hours already?” He muttered, the sound of his own voice startling him. Anastas floated to the observatory door and peeked in.

“Eternal life, post-scarcity, the utopia of our dreams and the dreams of our ancestors and their ancestors since time immemorial, it might finally be within our reach. And yet…”

“And yet, Gavriil?”

“And yet I fear you are right, Fyodor. I have spoken to the Americans. Most are eager to begin humanity’s new, great adventure into the stars. Most. I spoke to general Watchman. His father told him of realms we cannot possibly understand. We do not know what we are unleashing on our world.”

Anastas stared at the empty chair that the captain vanished from. The seat was hardly visible in the faint light of the stars through the observatory window. He floated to the chair and strapped himself into it and gazed out the window. The nearby red giant seemed farther away than before; the station seemed to be drifting further into deep space. Anastas glanced away from the window, and the darkness overwhelmed him. The station was dark, cold, and silent beyond a silence Anastas had ever known. The oppressive emptiness of space surrounded him and sucked the life and energy from him. The light from the stars without was his only comfort, and he found himself clinging to that comfort more and more desperately as the hours progressed. The conference table sat quiet for a long time while he was strapped to the chair.

Then the table began to glow once more. Anastas started. “Surely it hasn’t been twelve hours. No, they are coming faster.” He sighed. “Or perhaps I am losing sense of time.”

Captain Ivanov’s ghost settled in Anastas’ chair with a sigh. Anastas unstrapped himself and floated to the window as Major Dmitriyev materialized behind him.

“I don’t like this project, Gavriil…”

Anastas groaned and slammed his head against the window. “Every day. Every day!” He muttered. “‘I don’t like this, Gavriil.’ ‘I don’t like it, Fyodor.’ ‘We’re making a mistake.’ We’re making a mistake! Over and over and over and over and over again!” Anastas floated beside Major Dmitriyev. “And you go ‘I spoke to general Watchman. His father told him of realms we cannot possibly understand.’ But why? You did it anyways. And every time, when Captain’s watch says one twenty seven–”

Anastas stopped and stared. “Five thirty?” He said.

The ghost of Captain Ivanov stopped talking and stared up into Anastas’ eyes. The captain and the major vanished and everything went dark. But not silent.

Anastas shuddered and glanced nervously about the dark room. Lingering glow gave form to the furniture and the ridges in the walls. The slowing dancing light gave the illusion of movement to the objects scattered about. The sound of his stomach rumbling gave Anastas a start. There was no food in the station. The specter of starvation had already begun his slow, inevitable approach. Anastas noticed the dryness of his throat, and a faint, creeping odor of ammonia.

Ammonia?

Anastas floated out into the hall and immediately made his way to the service closet. The door to the room was cracked and the smell crept through the opening, a sharp odor that stung his nostrils and brought tears to his eyes. Anastas pulled the door open and immediately closed it.

He spun and pulled himself down the hall towards the other end, rubbing his eyes and cursing to himself the entire way. Nothing under the tables or in the shelves in the observatory was helpful to him. He moved to the comms room and rummaged around in the dark until he grasped a roll of tape in a cupboard. He grabbed one of the more lightweight EVA suits in the hall and slipped it on and sealed it. Grabbing a small spare oxygen tank, he hooked it to his suit as he floated down the hall and opened the door to the service closet. After a few seconds of fumbling in the dark, Anastas gave up and opened his suit to slip an arm out. The acrid air stung his lungs as he felt around the pipes and equipment, to no avail. He pulled himself out of the room and closed the door behind him.

Resting for a moment in the observatory, Anastas stared off into the starry cosmos and sighed. After a while, he remembered the flashlights attached to his EVA suit and went back to the closet to try again. He examined the coolant pipes and hoses, but everything seemed intact. Somewhere inside the walls of the station, beyond his reach, a pipe was leaking gas into the closet and flooding the station. Anastas closed the door behind him and slipped out of his EVA suit. Floating to the end of the hall, he grabbed one of the larger, bulkier suits, struggled into it, and detached the spare tank from his original suit. He found the lever for the hall airlock, turned, and saluted the empty hallway. With that, he opened the airlock and floated out into empty space.

He was facing the station, and there was a light in the observatory window. The ghost of Captain Ivanov walked to the window and looked out into space soberly. Anastas saw the pale entity slowly turn and watch him drift away vacantly, unblinking. Anastas turned as he separated from the station, until he saw only stars all around him, the full vastness of space an overwhelming sense that drew Anastas’ breath. He closed his eyes and breathed deeply to steady himself. When he opened them again, the stars had shifted. The station was gone. Everything was gone. The loneliness overtook him, and he reeled from vertigo. It seemed as if the stars themselves where shifting and moving around him, arranging themselves into shapes and constellations that circled him in dizzying formation. He blinked, and everything was still again.

Anastas glanced about the sphere around him, from one star to another, to another. Something felt off about the stars. He didn’t know how long he had been out here, time had left him long ago. A group of dimmer stars far away started flying across his vision relative to the others. It seemed to him as if they took the form of two giant eyes, many light-years away, watching him. Then the oxygen ran out.
